extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in fluid mechanics, computational scientists, and machine learning researchers applying ML to flow modeling, control, and optimization
extracted.subtask_description: A literature-review style set of guidelines and principles for applying machine learning (including GANs, RL, neural networks, sparse methods, etc.) to problems in fluid dynamics: modeling, reduced-order modeling, optimization, control, and experimental data processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) training objective and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The generative network produces candidate data to fool the discriminator; the discriminator provides labeled data and the loss is the Kullback–Leibler divergence between distributions. Training is adversarial (zero-sum), self-supervised, and may not guarantee convergence to equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about whether an equilibrium will be reached; large amounts of data help but there is no convergence guarantee. GANs can be used for super-resolution and dynamical-system inference, but the field is nascent for turbulence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinforcement learning (RL) framing and resource requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: RL frames goal-directed agent–environment interactions where the agent learns a policy π(s)=a and value function V(s) from rewards via trial-and-error without a priori labeled correct actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RL often requires very large numbers of episodes and significant computational resources—costs may be prohibitive for experiments and flow simulations. Applicable where trial-and-error interaction is possible; suitable for complex control/optimization tasks but plan for high compute and training-time expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term credit assignment (LTCA) and sparse rewards in RL
rubrics_metrics.description: LTCA is the challenge of inferring causal relations between long sequences of actions and delayed or sparse rewards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address LTCA by augmenting sparse objectives with densely-rewarded subgoals, using auxiliary tasks, or techniques to properly account for past experiences (e.g., replay buffers, hierarchical RL). Consider how reward design affects learning and required episode counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stochastic optimization as learning distributions (ES / GAs / EDAs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution Strategies and Genetic Algorithms iteratively construct probability distributions of design points that maximize objectives; CMA-ES adapts a Gaussian covariance matrix based on best points each iteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods are useful for black‑box, multimodal cost functions and highly parallelizable, but may require many evaluations and provide few convergence guarantees. Consider hybridizing with gradient methods or multi-fidelity models to reduce evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information-Geometric Optimization (IGO) and algorithm invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: IGO frameworks learn parameters of probability distributions during optimization while maintaining cost-function invariance as a design principle; flows can be equivalent to stochastic gradient descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IGO makes minimal assumptions on objective function shape. Effective on benchmarks but scaling and convergence in complex fluid-dynamics cost landscapes remain unclear—test carefully on problem-specific landscapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bayesian inference and Gaussian Processes (GaPs) for uncertainty quantification
rubrics_metrics.description: Bayesian inference provides full posterior distributions for model structure and parameters, fundamental for uncertainty quantification; Gaussian processes adapt kernels based on data and provide parameter distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bayesian methods give robust probabilistic predictions but are computationally costly (sampling/integration in high-dimensional spaces). Use as surrogates or for problems where UQ is critical and computational cost is manageable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of efficiency, accuracy, interpretability, and generalizability in modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeling goals should balance computational efficiency with predictive accuracy, while valuing interpretability and generalizability—especially in physics applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer models that provide hypotheses and insight (parsimonious models) when physics discovery is a goal. For engineering tasks, balance runtime constraints (e.g., real-time control) against fidelity needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensionality reduction: POD / PCA / autoencoders and interpolation vs extrapolation
rubrics_metrics.description: POD/PCA provide orthogonal linear modal decompositions; autoencoders (linear or nonlinear) produce latent embeddings. Deep networks can produce nonlinear coordinates but require large volumes of data and typically interpolate well, extrapolating poorly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use POD/PCA for interpretable linear reductions; use autoencoders for potentially more compact nonlinear embeddings with caution about extrapolation. Ensure training data cover intended operating regimes or expect limited generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clustering and classification: algorithm choice and interpretability
rubrics_metrics.description: Many clustering/classification algorithms exist; choose based on data size and desired number of categories. Cluster centroids can be linked to physical flow fields for interpretability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use k-means for partitioning phase space and to build low-dimensional Markov models; consider local reduced-order bases within clusters for robustness to parameter variations. Match algorithm to data characteristics (density, noise, labels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sparse and randomized methods for efficient computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Low-dimensional structure (sparsity, low-rank) enables compressed sensing and randomized linear algebra to accelerate computations (e.g., randomized SVD preserves structure with high probability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit sparsity and low-rank structure to decrease training/execution data needs and speed up matrix decompositions. Use randomized methods when matrices exhibit low-rank structure to gain large computational savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Super-resolution and de-noising tradeoffs and applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Super-resolution infers high-resolution fields from low-resolution measurements by leveraging statistical structure; approaches include example libraries, sparse representations, and CNNs. De-noising (flow cleansing) removes spurious vectors/outliers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Super-resolution is computationally costly but valuable when high-resolution measurements are impractical; GANs/CNNs have shown promise. Validate energy spectra and physical fidelity; be cautious of hallucinated structures outside training distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) and Koopman analysis limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: DMD extracts linear spatiotemporal coherent structures yielding low-dimensional linear evolution models; Koopman operator provides an (infinite-dimensional) linear description of observables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DMD assumes linear measurements and may fail to capture nonlinear transients; enrich with nonlinear measurements (extended DMD, kernel methods) or use deep learning to discover Koopman coordinates where dynamics appear linear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neural network modeling: interpolation, overfitting, cross-validation, and physics incorporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Neural networks are powerful but fundamentally interpolative and prone to overfitting; they work well when training data densely cover the task distribution. Explicitly incorporate physical properties (symmetries, constraints, conservation laws) where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-validate models on representative test sets, use regularization, and embed invariances (e.g., Galilean invariance) into architectures to improve generalization. Beware extrapolation beyond training distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimonious nonlinear models and model discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify minimal models that balance predictive accuracy with complexity (parsimony), using genetic programming, sparse regression in candidate libraries, and Pareto analysis to trade complexity against accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce physics constraints (e.g., conservation laws) when known; prefer sparse models when interpretability and generalizability are desired. Use Pareto fronts to select models with acceptable complexity and error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure modeling with machine learning and embedding invariances
rubrics_metrics.description: ML can model discrepancies in turbulence closures (e.g., Reynolds stress corrections); architectures can embed invariances (e.g., multiplicative layers to enforce Galilean invariance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate domain-specific invariances and tensor bases to ensure physically consistent predictions. Validate closures against high-fidelity simulations and test robustness across flow regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenges for ML in dynamical systems: interpretability, multi-scale dynamics, and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: ML for high-dimensional dynamical systems faces multi-scale dynamics, sensitivity to noise, latent variables, transients, and difficulty incorporating boundary conditions, symmetries, and global conservation laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize methods that can encode physics or constraints; augment ML with reduced-order or mechanistic models when possible. Evaluate models on interpretability and ability to generate testable hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of learning algorithms to flow optimization and control
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning algorithms (including RL and stochastic optimization) are suited to black-box or multimodal cost functions but are iterative and often require many more cost-function evaluations than gradient-based methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ML/stochastic methods when adjoint or gradient methods are applicable and efficient. Use ML when the cost landscape is nonconvex/black-box or when interacting with experiments; consider surrogates and multi-fidelity approaches to reduce evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrogate modeling and multi-fidelity strategies for optimization/control
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrogate models (e.g., neural networks) relate cost functions to control parameters and can be coupled with gradient methods; multi-fidelity algorithms combine inexpensive surrogates with expensive full evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build surrogates carefully to avoid local minima traps; update surrogates online as new data are acquired. Use multi-fidelity methods to balance accuracy and cost, and consider hybrid algorithms combining stochastic search and gradients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical deployment considerations: parallelism, experiments, convergence, and explainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Stochastic optimization and many ML methods are highly parallelizable and have been deployed in experimental and industrial settings, but convergence proofs, explainability, and reliability remain open issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deploying in experiments or industrial contexts, plan for massive parallel evaluations, instrument uncertainty handling, and provide safeguards for reliability and explainability. Consider hybrid or problem-specific combinations of methods.
